Balancing Speech, Language and Hearing Science with Machine Learning Modeling in the Age of AI: “Know your Problem, Data, and Solution”
abstract: The talk connects speech, language and hearing science with machine-learning modeling in the age of AI. It reviews how problem formulation, data, and solution design must stay coupled, contrasts earlier speech modeling with more recent innovations used in today's systems, and offers guidance for researchers entering the field. The take-home theme is: know your problem, know your data, and know your solution. Hansen's research has shaped speech recognition, speaker recognition and robust speech processing in noisy, stressed or emotional conditions, spanning speech production, speaker models, telecommunications, security/privacy, and assistive speech and hearing technologies.

title: The 5th ISCA-PECRAC Connecting Early Career Researchers and Social Gathering
Generalizable Speech Emotion Recognition: Strategies and Trends
abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) has traditionally been formulated as a discriminative learning problem over predefined emotion categories and has progressed tremendously under this paradigm. However, real-world emotion understanding requires models to generalize beyond the languages, emotion labels, speakers, and domains encountered during training. This talk surveys the evolving landscape of generalizable SER, highlighting strategies for cross-lingual and cross-domain transfer, adaptation to different emotion representations and taxonomies, and learning from increasingly diverse speech data. We then examine how recent advances in foundation models and speech large language models (Speech LLMs) are beginning to reshape the SER paradigm. These models offer new possibilities for reasoning about emotion beyond fixed label spaces. We conclude by discussing the emerging transition from task-specific SER toward flexible, multilingual, and potentially zero-shot, open-ended speech emotion understanding.

title: Monaural Speech Enhancement: From Shallow Networks to Speech Foundation Models
session_title: Neural Speech Enhancement: Survey, Diffusion and Flow Matching
abstract: This talk surveys single-channel neural speech enhancement, from its earliest shallow-learning approaches to today's speech foundation model era. We begin with the earliest attempts, which predate the deep learning era. We then move to the early mapping- and masking-based formulations in the time-frequency domain, where fully connected feed-forward neural networks first demonstrated the advantages of learned models over classical statistical estimators, and trace their architectural evolution. We next examine time-domain modeling, which bypasses explicit spectral representations entirely, before  turning to generative formulations that recast speech enhancement as distributional, sample-based generation of clean speech rather than deterministic regression/classification.  We conclude with the current frontier, where large, pre-trained speech models are repurposed for speech enhancement, and reflect on what this shift implies for evaluation, robustness, and the very notion of "clean" speech itself."

title: Pronunciation Diversity
abstract: Variability in natural speech is largely shaped by syntactic and pragmatic structure. Non-deterministic Generative Speech Models (GSMs), however, may produce intonation that diverges from these patterns. In the first part of this talk, I will review existing studies evaluating GSMs’ ability to simulate probabilistic intonational variation. The second part will focus on the Hindi discourse particle ‘-hii’, examining its pragmatic associations and intonational realizations in both human- and GSM-generated speech. I employ Functional Principal Component Analysis and Bayesian regression to characterize and compare intonational variability across the two sources. Using objective acoustic measures, I asses the extent to which contemporary GSMs capture naturally occurring intonational variability and its pragmatic conditioning. Overall, this talk aims to highlight both the potential and the limitations of GSMs for generating pragmatically appropriate spoken language.

title: Speech Technology and Linguistic Diversity
Low-Resource Speech Synthesis: What Have We Solved, and What Remains?
abstract: Speech synthesis has traditionally required substantial amounts of transcribed speech, limiting its availability to only a fraction of the world’s languages. Multilingual and cross-lingual transfer, learning from unpaired data, unsupervised speech-unit discovery, and more recently foundation models have dramatically reduced these requirements. Today, models can synthesize hundreds or even thousands of languages, sometimes with little or no transcribed speech in the target language. This talk surveys the key advances behind this progress and highlights what has been successfully addressed in low-resource speech synthesis. It then examines what remains challenging, particularly for genuinely under-resourced languages, including linguistic diversity, synthesis quality, and reliable evaluation. Finally, drawing on experiences from Indigenous and endangered language technology, I discuss how future progress can better connect advances in speech synthesis with the needs and priorities of language communities.

title: Recent advances in speech language model for ASR
abstract: With recent advances in large language models (LLMs), both academia and industry have increasingly focused on developing speech LLMs by integrating the speech modality into LLM architectures. This talk centers on recent progress in speech-LLM for automatic speech recognition (ASR). While standard speech-LLM approaches have reached maturity, as evidenced by state-of-the-art results on major leaderboards, I will delve into topics such as unleashing the full potential of LLMs, long-form speech modeling, and decoding acceleration. I will also introduce recent breakthroughs in encoder-free speech-LLMs, which pave the way toward truly native multimodal language models that process speech as naturally as text.

title: Clinically meaningful speech representations
abstract: While modern speech models can learn powerful representations that achieve impressive predictive performance, high accuracy alone has not translated into widespread clinical adoption. Bridging this gap requires representations that are interpretable, robust across populations, tasks, languages, and recording conditions, sensitive to clinically meaningful change, reliable across participants longitudinally, validated against relevant clinical constructs and outcomes, and ultimately, used to support decisions in real-world studies. This talk surveys the evolution of clinically meaningful speech representations, illustrating key developments with examples from research across ALS, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, depression, autism, and cognitive impairment. We will examine approaches and challenges to combining the power of state-of-the-art models, composite measures and scalable multimodal assessment on the one hand with interpretability, psychometric rigor, and clinical validation on the other in order to transform speech representations from merely being compelling lab research into becoming useful real-world clinical tools.

title: Low-Resource & Endangered Language Speech Processing
abstract: Current speech AI covers ~100 languages among >5000 languages in the world.  The remaining languages are essentially low-resourced, and many of them are in danger of extinction.  However, speech technology will be useful for preservation and revival of these languages. This talk overviews the approaches, datasets, training method, available foundation models, and use cases of speech recognition and synthesis for these languages, including the Ainu and Ryukyuan project conducted by the presenter's group.

title: To be announced (Survey Talk, 40 mins)
Beyond Text-to-Music: Control, Agency, and Evaluation in Generative Audio
abstract: Generative audio has rapidly expanded from speech synthesis to music, singing, environmental sound, instrument synthesis, and audio production. This talk surveys this landscape for the speech community, connecting music and audio generation to familiar problems such as TTS, voice conversion, enhancement, source separation, prosody modeling, and neural vocoding. We will review audio language models built on neural codecs, diffusion and flow-matching methods, Transformer generators, and differentiable DSP methods. The central theme is control. Text prompts are accessible but musically ambiguous; creators also need interpretable and editable representations such as MIDI, lyrics, stems, reference audio clips, and synthesizer knobs. We will examine tasks including text-to-music, singing synthesis, Foley, continuation, inpainting, stem-conditioned generation, symbolic modeling, and generative enhancement. We conclude with evaluation: why perceptual quality and Fréchet distances are insufficient, and how conditioning adherence, musical coherence, and creative agency can guide future interactive music tools.

title: What does it mean to ‘know a word’?
AI in Communication Sciences: Necessity, Opportunity or Threat?
presenter: John H. L. Hansen, Emma Power, Visar Berisha, Karen Hirschausen, Brendan Lonergan, Nicky Chong-White (Facilitator)
abstract: Bringing together experts from research and clinical practice, this session will put the opportunities, risks and realities of AI in speech pathology and audiology up for debate. From its potential to improve care and accessibility to the ethical, professional and implementation challenges it presents, expect differing perspectives, challenging questions and a lively debate on what AI should, and should not, mean for the future of the field.

title: On the challenges and benefits of dynamic vowel analyses
abstract: The aim of this presentation is to give an overview of recent studies dealing with the dynamics of monophthongs, diphthongs, and hiatus sequences. Traditionally, monophthongs have been defined by their steady states, but especially in continuous and non-laboratory speech, steady states are often hard to identify given increased articulatory blending. Vowel-vowel-sequences, on the other hand, have long been recognized as inherently dynamic, but for reasons of complexity reduction and computational efficiency, they are still often analyzed in terms of static metrics such as DCT coefficients or the rate of change of the formants. In this presentation, I will show how novel methodological approaches to dynamic analyses can provide new insights into vowels and vowel sequences, but also discuss under which circumstances a more straight-forward, static analysis suffices.

title: Bio-Informed Speech Processing, Modeling, and Generation
abstract: Survey talk opening the Modeling Articulation oral session. The official program grid preserves the title but not a full abstract in the exported sheet. Treat it as a survey of biologically informed approaches to speech processing, articulatory modeling, and generation, and do not invent specific claims, datasets, or results.

title: Factorization and Latent Structure in Speech Representations
abstract: Structure in speech representations facilitates controlled generation, transfer to new domains, and analysis of model behavior. This talk surveys methods for imposing and discovering structure in speech representations. We give an overview of top-down techniques for imposing structure on learned representations, including the use of factorized training objectives, model distillation, and explicit bottlenecks or interpretable control variables. We discuss the advantages and limitations of this approach and contrast them with bottom-up techniques, including probing, controlled perturbations, latent-space arithmetic, and resynthesis, for discovering and exploiting pre-existing structure in large pre-trained models. We conclude by discussing applications enabled by such structure, including controllable generation and editing, voice conversion, domain transfer, efficient speech modeling, and the separation or attribution of multiple speakers.

title: Expressive Speech Translation
session_title: Information Extraction and Retrieval / Survey Talk
abstract: Speech to speech translation is still a challenging problem, without much consensus about model architectures, training data, evaluation methods, and so on. One frontier in this area is the preservation of the expressiveness of the input speech in the translation. Expressiveness ranges from global properties such as the speaker's voice and emotion as well as acoustic conditions, to local properties such as pauses, varying speaking rates, emphasis, and pitch for individual words. This survey will cover various aspects, such as training data, data synthesis methods, speech representation, model architectures, the use of large language models, and evaluation metrics.

title: One Embedding Doesn't Fit All: Rethinking Speaker Modeling Robustness Across Speaker-Centric Tasks
abstract: Speaker embeddings have become a fundamental representation for a wide range of speaker-centric speech applications, including speaker verification, diarization, target speaker extraction, and personalized speech interaction. However, a speaker representation optimized for one task or acoustic condition does not necessarily generalize well to others. This survey revisits the notion of robustness in speaker modeling from a broader, task-oriented perspective. We review recent progress in learning speaker representations under variations in acoustics, speech content, duration, and domain, and discuss how speaker information is exploited differently across downstream tasks. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs between task-independent speaker representations and task-adaptive modeling. Finally, we highlight emerging challenges and opportunities toward more generalizable, transferable, and task-aware speaker modeling for future speech and multimodal systems.

title: Mitigating Pruning-Quantization Compound Errors for Ultra-Lightweight ResNet34-Based Speaker Recognition
abstract: While deep neural networks (DNNs) have greatly advanced speaker recognition, backbone models such as ResNet34 still suffer from computation and memory footprints, making difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices. To this end, we explored pruning and quantization techniques to compress speaker recognition model. Specifically, we propose a unified compression framework that combines channel pruning and low-bit quantization. Specifically, we propose ResRep-MB, a pruning strategy with multi-branch compactors for accurate channel importance assessment, achieving near-lossless structural compression. To mitigate the compound errors caused by pruning and INT4 quantization, we propose Progressive Pruning-Quantization Distillation (PPQD), which employs a dual-teacher mechanism. Experiments on VoxCeleb1 and CN-Celeb1 demonstrate that the compressed ResNet34 achieves a 19.2× compression ratio with only a 6.8% relative EER degradation, while maintaining robust cross-language performance.
